thread.title: GoPro: For CEO Nick Woodman, It’s Been a ‘Journey’

author: David Marino-Nachison
title: GoPro: For CEO Nick Woodman, It’s Been a ‘Journey’
text:
Photo: GoPro By David Marino-Nachison Updated July 30, 2018 9:06 a.m. ET GoPro (GPRO) was one of 2014’s hottest IPOs, is shares rising some 130% in the months after its May listing. Since then, they’ve given up all of those gains — and much more.
The reason: The company’s growth story fell apart . Revenues in 2017 were the lowest since 2013, and GoPro has been in the red since 2015. The shares closed last week at around $6; their post IPO-high was near $94.
Newsletter Sign-up These days, the Barron’s Next 50 company wants to convince investors that it has learned from past mistakes, refocused its product line, and restored spending discipline. In January, it announced a dramatic restructuring in an attempt to turn things around.
And CEO Nick Woodman is explaining what he calls his “entrepreneur’s journey,” during which he says he’s realized GoPro must be guided by information instead of intuition, built rather than dreamed into being.
“When we took the company public, I believed that part of my job was to envision this ultimate version of GoPro—what it could ultimately become—using all of my imagination,” Woodman, 43, said in a recent interview with Barron’s Next. “But we thought that we were really smarter and more creative than we were.”
This year started with the January announcement of more than 250 job cuts, bringing the company’s head count below 1,000, and the demise of the Karma drone line.
Since then, the company has reworked its Plus subscription service, which includes unlimited photo storage and “no questions asked” replacement cameras; launched a $199 entry-level Hero camera and a “trade-up” program for older models; and announced a feature that lets users share content directly to Facebook ’s (FB) Instagram.
It also updated the software on the $699 Fusion camera , a 360-degree recording device that illustrates how the company believes its higher-end cameras can be a kind of laboratory for future products even as the $199, $299 and $399 price points continue to represent its core offering .
”In the ‘prosumer’ realm, we can introduce experiences that are fabulously convenient for that user but are still getting there for the mass market,” he said, saying 360-degree cameras have “the potential to be the most automatic foolproof experience sharing solution for consumers.”
Our experience perhaps illustrates that point. Earlier this year, we took a Fusion—lent, along with an Apple (AAPL) iPhone preloaded with GoPro software, by the company—on a ski trip to the western U.S. We told the company we were GoPro novices, wanting to make sure the device got a fair shot; they insisted we’d be OK.
They were right. Still, getting started, taking good shots and turning them into usable content required some trial and error in terms of when and where to shoot, where best to mount a camera on a helmet, how to effectively use the included selfie stick/tripod, and how much video to download at one time.
User error and inexperience aside, all of that could be made even simpler, which Woodman believes it will.
“We see that product becoming smaller, more convenient and ultimately more appealing to the mass market,” he said. “It’ll take a real knucklehead to take a bad shot with a Fusion in the future.”
The effects of GoPro’s efforts remain to be seen. In May, the company reported first-quarter financial results that showed revenue falling year-over-year but unit sales ticking upward—a sign, the company believes, that consumers like its offerings.
“Our time-tested good-better-best product strategy is working once again,” Woodman said during a May conference call with investors, a transcript of which is available on SeekingAlpha .
The company is scheduled to announce second-quarter financial results on August 2 ; Wall Street expects a net loss of $0.22 per share on revenue of $270 million, according to FactSet, with both estimates below year-ago levels.
The second half is generally more important to GoPro; this year, especially the fourth quarter, should be particularly so, with the company planning a revamp of its core product line for the first time in roughly half a decade. Wall Street predicts year-over-year revenue growth in Q4.
Woodman says better manufacturing and sourcing should make the new models more profitable while offering consumers the same value.
And GoPro is now plumbing its historic sales data for insights about consumer desires and buying behaviors, and more strategic—and, perhaps, frequent—refreshes of GoPro’s product and price lineup are likely, according to Woodman.
“You need new products every year,” he said. “And If you leave a product out, you have to discount that product by $100 if you want to drive sales.”
More About Barron’s Next Learn more about Barron’s Next The Barron’s Next 50 Investors remain wary. GoPro’s shares are off some 17% in 2018, underperforming the S&P 500. The mean share price target is currently at $5.54, according to FactSet, about 10% below current levels; none of the analysts covering the company have “buy” recommendations on the stock.
Some investors may be holding out hope that GoPro is acquired, which Woodman has said the company would consider . Lately, however, it’s been pretty quiet on the merger rumor front. GoPro’s outward focus is on its products—earlier this month, it said it sold its 30 millionth HD camera in the second quarter—and, for Woodman, on its process.
“You need to make something out of nothing” as an entrepreneur, Woodman said. “But from the very moment you put your product or service out in the market, the market begins telling you what it wants your product or service to be. You either listen to that or you remain a creator, and each of your creations is a bet on the market wanting it.”
Meanwhile, Woodman — at times portrayed as a Red Bull-chugging swashbuckler — can now be easily drawn into a brainstorming session about how best to record the antics of his children, rather than extreme athletes. (Though he also recently took a surf vacation; that’s him in the photo that tops this story.)
“When you have something your kids really want from you, and they try to get it, and they can’t get it,” he mused during our interview, “put the Fusion in the tripod, on the ground, and then he chases you…”
When the idea finally ran its course, the father — Woodman has three young sons — once again became the pitchman. “With Fusion,” he said, “your ability to capture those types of experiences is unrivaled.”
